challenges.name: openapi-versioning-deprecation
challenges.title: OpenAPI, versioning and deprecation
challenges.description: Three statements on the CodeDev API's generated OpenAPI document, its versioning policy and the headers of a deprecated field.

questions.explanation: True. @nestjs/swagger builds the document from decorators and class metadata, not from what the handler returns at run time. The cast tells TypeScript the string is a number, so neither the compiler nor the generator sees the problem: the document promises an integer and the API sends a string. Code-first generation keeps the document close to the code but does not test it; validating real responses (or responses from the app in memory) against the document closes the gap. The misconception is that a generated spec is correct by construction.

questions.question:
docs/api-versioning-policy.md (CodeDev API):
1. The major version is in the URL: /v1/... . A new major version is only for a redesign that cannot be made compatible.
2. Within /v1, additive changes (new endpoints, new optional request fields, new response properties) ship without notice.
3. Breaking changes within /v1 follow expand/contract: deprecate, announce with Deprecation and Sunset headers and a changelog entry, remove after the sunset date (at least 90 days for partner endpoints).

Pull request #530: adds the response property "estimatedHours" (integer) to GET /v1/courses/{slug}.

Statement: "Under this policy, pull request #530 has to wait for /v2 because it changes the response of a /v1 endpoint."
questions.explanation: False. Rule 2 says new response properties are additive changes that ship within /v1, and for response readers a new property is safe (as long as clients ignore unknown keys, which the policy implies by calling it additive). A new major version is reserved for changes that cannot be made compatible (rule 1). Teams that open /v2 for every change end up running several versions that each need fixes, tests and documentation. The misconception is that any change to a response is a change of version.

questions.question:
$ curl -sI https://api.codedev.test/v1/courses/api-design-production
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Deprecation: @1792746000
Sunset: Mon, 30 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT
Link: <https://api.codedev.test/docs/changes/2026-10-course-dto>; rel="deprecation"

Statement: "A client can learn from this response alone that something in it is deprecated (since 23 Oct 2026, 09:00 UTC), the date after which it is expected to stop working, and where to read the migration notice."
questions.explanation: True. Deprecation (RFC 9745) carries the deprecation date as @ plus Unix seconds: 1792746000 is 23 Oct 2026, 09:00 UTC. Sunset (RFC 8594) carries the date after which the resource or feature is expected to stop working, as an HTTP-date. The Link with rel="deprecation" points to human-readable information. A client library or an API gateway can log or alert on these headers without anyone reading the changelog. The headers do not say which fields are deprecated; that is what the notice and the deprecated flags in the OpenAPI document are for. The misconception is that deprecation only lives in documentation that clients must remember to read.
